Identifiability and Failure Modes

Theory, Chapter 8

theory-08-identifiability-and-failure-modes.Rmd

What identifiability means

A parameter is identifiable if different values of that parameter imply different distributions over observable data. If two distinct parameter configurations produce exactly the same likelihood for all possible datasets, the parameters are not identifiable. The data cannot distinguish between them, regardless of sample size, estimation method, or computational resources.

This definition concerns information, not estimation. An identifiable parameter may still be difficult to estimate (requiring large samples, careful priors, or specialised algorithms). An unidentifiable parameter cannot be estimated at all, in any principled sense. No amount of data resolves the ambiguity because there is no ambiguity to resolve: the likelihood surface is flat in the relevant direction.

In hierarchical models with latent structure, identifiability becomes more complex. The parameters of interest include not just fixed effects or variance components but the entire latent configuration (the values of unobserved quantities at each unit). Some of these quantities may be well-identified; others may be weakly constrained; still others may be fundamentally underdetermined given the model structure.

The previous chapters established that SIMP operates through latent structure: ecological variation lives in an unconstrained latent space, and observations are constrained projections of that space. This architecture creates identifiability properties that must be understood, not assumed away.

The scale ambiguity

The observation model maps latent values to constrained proportions. This mapping involves normalisation: the cover allocated to each present species depends on relative latent values.

Consider a simple case. Suppose two species are present in a plot, with latent values λ1\lambda_1 and λ2\lambda_2. The cover allocation depends on how these values compare (perhaps through a softmax or similar transformation). If we shift both values by the same constant, the relative comparison is unchanged. If we scale both values by the same factor, the relative comparison may also be unchanged, depending on the functional form.

This creates a scale ambiguity. The data constrain relative latent values but not their absolute level. A configuration where all latent values are high produces the same observable proportions as one where all are low, provided the relative structure is preserved.

Not a defect of any particular parameterisation. Structural. The simplex constraint means that only ratios matter for allocation. The absolute scale of latent values is not identified by cover data alone.

In practice, this ambiguity is resolved through constraints: fixing one latent value to a reference, using sum-to-zero constraints, or imposing priors that anchor the scale. These constraints are assumptions. They make the model formally identified but do not add information. The data remain silent about absolute scale; the constraints substitute a modelling decision for missing information.

Weak identification from absence

Chapter 4 established that zeros are structural features of cover data, not nuisances. Chapter 5 noted that latent values for absent species are weakly informed. This section makes the identifiability implications explicit.

When a species is absent from a plot, the data tell us that its latent value was “low enough” to produce absence. Depending on the observation model, this may mean the value fell below some threshold, or that the probability of presence given the latent value was low. Either way, the observation is censored: we learn that the latent value is in some region, but not where within that region.

A fundamental asymmetry. For present species, cover values constrain latent values relatively tightly (higher cover implies higher relative latent value). For absent species, the constraint is one-sided and weak. The latent value could be slightly below the presence threshold or far below it; the data do not distinguish.

When zeros dominate (when most species are absent from most plots) most latent values are weakly identified. The full latent configuration has high dimension, but the data inform only a small fraction of it. The remainder is determined by assumptions: the prior distribution over latent values, the structure imposed by covariates, the dependence structure that borrows information across units.

Not a problem to be solved. A property of the data structure. Absence is less informative than presence. A framework that represents zeros honestly must also represent the limits of what zeros can tell us.

Confounding between presence and allocation

The SIMP framework separates two processes: which species are present, and how cover is allocated among present species. Both processes depend on latent values. This creates potential for confounding.

Consider a covariate (say, soil moisture) that affects both presence and allocation. Wetter sites may have higher probability of certain species being present, and among present species, wetter sites may allocate more cover to moisture-loving species. The covariate acts on both stages.

The two effects are not independently identified. If we observe that a species has high cover in wet plots, this could reflect: (a) higher presence probability in wet plots, so the species appears in more wet plots; (b) higher allocation in wet plots, so the species gets more cover when present; or (c) both. The observed pattern is consistent with multiple combinations of presence and allocation effects.

This confounding is intrinsic to the two-stage structure. The stages are not observed separately. We observe the final cover, which reflects the composition of both processes. Separating their contributions requires either: strong assumptions about how they differ in form, additional data that informs one stage independently, or acceptance that only the combined effect is identified.

The confounding is particularly severe when zeros are common. With few observations of presence, the presence model is estimated from limited data. The allocation model is estimated only from plots where the species occurs. The two sources of information may be nearly non-overlapping for rare species.

Flat regions in the likelihood

The likelihood function summarises what the data say about parameters. In well-identified models, the likelihood has a clear peak: moving away from the maximum reduces the likelihood substantially. In weakly identified models, the likelihood surface has flat regions, directions along which the likelihood changes little or not at all.

For compositional data with latent structure, flat regions arise from several sources.

Scale invariance. As noted above, normalisation removes information about absolute scale. The likelihood is constant along directions that shift all latent values uniformly.

Absent species. Latent values for absent species are constrained only to be “low.” The likelihood varies weakly across configurations that satisfy this constraint.

Exchangeable structure. If latent values share a common distribution with estimated variance, the data constrain the variance but not individual deviations from the mean. Many configurations of individual values are consistent with the same variance estimate.

Dependence parameters. Structured dependence (spatial, group-level) introduces parameters controlling how latent values covary. When most values are weakly identified individually, the covariance structure is also weakly identified. The data may constrain the overall strength of dependence but not its detailed form.

These flat regions are not numerical artefacts. Properties of the information structure. The likelihood is genuinely uninformative about certain aspects of the parameter space.

Ridges and near-ridges

Distinct from flat regions are ridges: directions along which different parameter combinations yield nearly identical likelihoods. Ridges indicate trade-offs. If one parameter increases, another can compensate to maintain the same fit.

In hierarchical models, common ridges include:

Mean-variance trade-offs. A model with higher latent mean and higher variance may fit comparably to one with lower mean and lower variance. The data constrain a combination of these quantities but not each separately.

Intercept-covariate trade-offs. A model with a high intercept and negative covariate effect may fit comparably to one with a lower intercept and less negative effect. The data constrain fitted values, not the decomposition into components.

Individual-group trade-offs. In hierarchical models, variation can be attributed to individual-level deviations or group-level effects. The total variation is constrained; its partition is not.

Ridges create practical difficulties for estimation: algorithms may wander along them, and posterior distributions may be elongated or multimodal. But the underlying issue is informational. The data do not contain enough information to resolve the trade-off. Any resolution comes from assumptions: priors, constraints, or regularisation.

How structured dependence can mislead

Chapter 6 established that structured dependence belongs at the latent level. Chapter 7 established that any finite representation of dependence is a modelling commitment. This section addresses how dependence structure interacts with identifiability.

Structured dependence borrows information across units. If latent values at nearby plots are assumed similar, observations at one plot inform estimates at its neighbours. This borrowing can improve estimates when the assumption is correct and the data are sparse.

But borrowing is not learning. It propagates assumptions as much as it propagates data. If the dependence structure is misspecified (if the true process has different range, different smoothness, or different geometry than assumed) the borrowed information is systematically wrong.

The identifiability concern: misspecification may not be detectable. A model with the wrong dependence structure can still fit the data well if it adjusts other parameters to compensate. The data may not distinguish between: (a) strong local dependence with weak covariate effects, and (b) weak dependence with strong covariate effects. Both can produce similar patterns of spatial similarity in the fitted values.

This confounding between dependence and fixed effects is well-known in spatial statistics. Not unique to compositional data. But compositional data exacerbate it because the weak identification of absent species means there is less information to discipline the dependence structure. The dependence parameters are estimated primarily from present species, which may be a biased or unrepresentative subset.

Why more data does not always help

A natural response to identifiability concerns is to collect more data. More plots, more species, more covariates. For some limitations, this helps. For others, it does not.

More data helps when the limitation is statistical uncertainty, when the parameter is identified but estimated imprecisely due to small samples. Additional observations tighten confidence intervals and resolve ambiguity.

More data does not help when the limitation is structural. If two parameter configurations produce identical likelihoods for all possible datasets, more observations from the same data-generating process provide no new information. The configurations remain indistinguishable.

For SIMP, several limitations are structural:

  • The scale ambiguity is resolved by constraints, not by data.
  • The weak identification of absent species’ latent values is a property of censoring, not sample size. Adding more plots where the species is absent does not inform its latent value; only plots where it is present do.
  • Confounding between presence and allocation is a property of the two-stage structure, not the number of observations.
  • Confounding between dependence and fixed effects depends on the design (how covariates vary in space), not just the number of units.

This does not mean data collection is futile. Data collection should be strategic, targeting the specific identifiability limitations that affect the scientific question. More of the same data may not resolve ambiguities that are structural in nature.

The role of assumptions

In regions where the likelihood is flat or nearly flat, inference is determined by assumptions. In Bayesian terms, the posterior reflects the prior. In frequentist terms, estimates are determined by constraints or regularisation rather than data.

This is how inference works in partially identified models. The honest response: acknowledge which components are informed by data and which by assumptions, and assess sensitivity to those assumptions.

For SIMP, key assumptions that fill identifiability gaps include:

Prior distributions on latent values. These determine the baseline level and spread of latent values when the data are uninformative. For absent species, the prior is doing most of the work.

Prior distributions on variance components. These determine how variation is partitioned when the data do not strongly constrain the partition.

The form of the dependence structure. Assuming spatial smoothness, exchangeable groups, or independence is a substantive choice that affects estimates even in data-rich settings.

The observation model linking latent values to cover. The functional form of this mapping affects which latent configurations are consistent with observed data.

These assumptions are structural components of the model that determine behaviour in weakly identified regions. A user who does not examine sensitivity to these assumptions does not understand what the model is doing.

Failure modes

The identifiability properties described above produce characteristic failure modes. Not bugs or rare pathologies. Predictable consequences of the framework’s structure.

Overconfident inference about rare species. For species absent from most plots, the apparent precision of estimates reflects the prior more than the data. Narrow credible intervals may indicate strong prior assumptions, not strong data support.

Unstable covariate effects. When presence-allocation confounding is severe, estimated covariate effects may be sensitive to modelling choices (which covariates are included, how the observation model is specified, what priors are used). Different defensible choices yield different conclusions.

Spatial smoothing that masks local heterogeneity. If the dependence structure assumes smooth spatial variation, local discontinuities or heterogeneity will be smoothed away. The model will produce smooth maps even when the underlying process is patchy.

Apparent covariate effects that reflect spatial confounding. If a covariate varies spatially and the dependence structure is misspecified, the covariate may absorb variation that should be attributed to spatial structure, or vice versa. The estimated effect conflates multiple sources.

Posterior multimodality or poor mixing. When ridges or flat regions are present, sampling algorithms may fail to explore the posterior. Apparent convergence may mask unvisited regions of comparable posterior density.

These failure modes are not always diagnosable from standard outputs. A model may fit well, produce smooth predictions, and yield narrow uncertainty intervals while suffering from one or more of these issues. The failures are failures of interpretation and generalisation, not of fit.

What this means for use

This chapter has catalogued limitations, not solutions. The purpose: establish what the framework can and cannot deliver.

SIMP is informative about:

  • Relative latent values among present species within plots.
  • Overall patterns of presence across species and plots, given assumptions about presence thresholds.
  • Combined effects of covariates on cover, integrating presence and allocation.
  • Broad patterns of spatial or group-level similarity, given assumptions about dependence structure.

SIMP is weakly informative about:

  • Absolute latent values (resolved only by constraints).
  • Latent values for absent species (resolved primarily by priors).
  • Separate contributions of presence and allocation to covariate effects.
  • Fine-scale spatial structure when data are sparse.

SIMP is silent about:

  • Whether the dependence structure is correctly specified.
  • Whether apparent covariate effects reflect confounding with unmeasured spatial structure.
  • Whether apparent precision reflects data or prior assumptions.

A user who understands these boundaries can use the framework appropriately, interpret outputs cautiously, and recognise when conclusions are robust versus fragile. A user who does not understand them risks mistaking assumption-driven results for data-driven conclusions.

Summary

Identifiability in SIMP is partial and uneven. Some components of the latent structure are well-constrained by data; others are weakly informed; still others are determined entirely by assumptions.

The scale of latent values is not identified; fixed by convention. The latent values of absent species are weakly identified; determined primarily by priors. The separation of presence and allocation effects is not identified when both processes share covariates. The dependence structure confounds with fixed effects when covariates vary spatially.

These limitations are structural. They arise from the geometry of constrained observations, the censoring induced by zeros, and the architecture of hierarchical models. They cannot be eliminated by better algorithms, larger samples, or more careful implementation.

The appropriate response is transparency. Users should understand which aspects of their inference are data-driven and which are assumption-driven. Sensitivity analyses should probe the assumptions that matter. Conclusions should be calibrated to the strength of the evidence, not the precision of the output.

This chapter does not propose solutions to these limitations. It establishes that they exist, that they are intrinsic to the framework, and that ignoring them leads to misuse. A framework that is honest about its limits is more trustworthy than one that obscures them.
